slides.0.title: Côte des Bar and the outer areas
slides.0.subtitle: Aube Pinot Noir, Les Riceys and the frontiers of Champagne
slides.1.title: Position and scale of the Côte des Bar
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Position
slides.1.highlights.0.content: In the Aube south-east of Troyes, about 130 km from the centre of Champagne, on the same Kimmeridgian marl belt as Chablis (WineWithSeth)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Area and villages
slides.1.highlights.1.content: About 7,900 ha and 64 villages (2022, via WineWithSeth; elsewhere about 8,000 ha and 63 villages), with the Aube holding about 23% of the region (Comité Champagne). Sources differ, so not tested
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Varieties
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Pinot Noir is about 83% (another source says 86%) with minor Chardonnay and Meunier; the figure differs, so only remember that Pinot Noir dominates
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Soils
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Mostly Jurassic Kimmeridgian clay-limestone marl with Portlandian debris in places, unlike the chalk of the central Champagne
slides.1.content: Pinot Noir plus Kimmeridgian: the Champagne that borders northern Burgundy.
slides.2.title: History, sub-zones and climate
slides.2.highlights.0.title: A bumpy delimitation
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Excluded from the 1908 delimitation, restored in 1911 as a second zone and fully included by the law of 22 July 1927 (WineWithSeth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: No Grand or Premier Cru
slides.2.highlights.1.content: All 17 + 42 villages in the INAO list are in the Marne; the Aube has none, so the Côte des Bar sits outside the village hierarchy
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Two sub-zones
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The Seine and Aube rivers split the area into the larger western Bar-sur-Seine (Barséquanais) and the smaller eastern Bar-sur-Aube (Bar-sur-Aubois)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: A warmer setting
slides.2.highlights.3.content: About 1°C warmer than central Champagne with over 100 more sunshine hours a year (WineWithSeth, single source, not tested), helping Pinot Noir ripen
slides.2.content: Detailed figures for sub-zones, area and climate come from single sources, so the teaching focus is position, variety and no classification.
slides.3.title: Les Riceys and distinctive places
slides.3.highlights.0.title: One village, three AOCs
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Les Riceys can produce Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys, chosen by the grower at vinification; at about 866 ha it is the largest wine-growing village in Champagne (WineWithSeth)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Rosé des Riceys
slides.3.highlights.1.content: An AOC since 8 December 1947 (WineWithSeth); Pinot Noir only, still rosé; the INAO specification (2026 draft) requires whole-bunch semi-carbonic maceration and at least 10% natural alcohol, with vineyards limited to Les Riceys
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Producers and specialities
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Drappier in Urville and Devaux in Bar-sur-Seine are leading producers; the Celles-sur-Ource area is known for Pinot Blanc
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Montgueux
slides.3.highlights.3.content: A chalky hill west of Troyes on Turonian chalk, almost all Chardonnay; it is a region of its own in INAO's divisions, not part of the Côte des Bar (WineWithSeth)
slides.3.content: Rosé des Riceys is tiny (about 50,000 to 150,000 bottles, under 0.05% of regional output), so the point is to recognise its name and rules.
slides.4.title: Outer areas and the five départements
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Five départements
slides.4.highlights.0.content: The appellation spans the Marne, Aube, Aisne, Haute-Marne and Seine-et-Marne, with 319 crus (Comité Champagne)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Côte de Sézanne
slides.4.highlights.1.content: In the southern Marne, roughly parallel to the Côte des Blancs but further south, mainly planted to Chardonnay (WineWithSeth)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Around Vitry-le-François
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The specification says the delimited parcels in this arrondissement were approved at the INAO meeting of 7–8 November 1990, and that in some communes (such as Brienne-le-Château and Épagne) no parcel was retained
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Aisne, Haute-Marne and Seine-et-Marne
slides.4.highlights.3.content: The Aisne holds about 10% (the western continuation of the Marne valley) while the Haute-Marne and Seine-et-Marne are very small; official département shares are not published and sources differ, so not tested
slides.4.content: The outer areas are small but D3 often asks about the edges of Champagne.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the main variety of the Côte des Bar (Aube)?
Pinot Noir makes up over eight tenths (the exact share varies by source).
Where are the Grand Cru and Premier Cru villages of the INAO list located?
A. All in the Marne département
B. In the Marne and the Aube
All 17 + 42 villages are in the Marne; the Aube has none.
Which variety is used for Rosé des Riceys?
C. A blend of Pinot Noir and Meunier
INAO specification: Pinot Noir only, as a still rosé.
